newsitem.title: ZAIRE: New Congo breaks up protest, blames reactionaries.
newsitem.headline: New Congo breaks up protest, blames reactionaries.

text.p: Troops in Kinshasa fired in the air on Saturday to break up a march by about 1,000 students protesting against self-proclaimed president Laurent Kabila's new government.

Some 100 demonstrators were loaded onto trucks and taken to Kinshasa's Camp Kololo military barracks. The new authorities blamed reactionary political forces and said demonstrations were technically banned.

"In principle demonstrations have not been permitted in all parts of the country that we have liberated in this period of consolidation, but we are very tolerant," Information Minister Raphael Ghenda told Reuters.
"Today what happened is that reactionary political forces of the former regime manipulated people who claimed to be students."
Witnesses said the students taken to the barracks near the city centre were not seen coming out.
"I can assure you that the order had to be maintained and that after some people were removed from the street they were taken straight to their homes," Ghenda said.

Marching a week after Kabila's forces took the capital from soldiers loyal to ousted President Mobutu Sese Seko, the students were protesting against the exclusion of opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi from the new government and the presence of Rwandan and other African troops.

Kabila's rebellion, which was triggered by ethnic Tutsis demanding citizenship, has received military assistance from Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army, Western intelligence sources and most Congolese people say.
Mobutu, weakened by cancer, arrived in Morocco on Friday from Togo but an official in Rabat said on Saturday he was expected to go on to France early next month.
With anti-Kabila anger spreading to Tshisekedi's homeland in the centre of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Kabila's admirers in Kinshasa staged a symbolic show of support.
A march by about 150 Kabila supporters was allowed to go ahead unhindered.

Residents in Mbuji-Mayi, the diamond mining capital of Tshisekedi's Kasai homeland, said protesters were dispersed by Kabila's soldiers on Friday. Mbuji-Mayi was calm on Saturday with businesses open.
In announcing his incomplete government on Thursday, Kabila not only excluded Tshisekedi but also abolished the post of prime minister -- which the radical politician claims.

Saturday's Potentiel newspaper said the people of the new Congo feared a return to dictatorship. "They see from the first political acts of the new rulers that we are heading towards a single party state," it said.
Borders remained closed on Saturday, but Transport Minister Henri Mova said there was no technical reason for the measure and that regular flights could start by Tuesday.
Mova told a news conference that security considerations were to blame for the fact that travellers had been stopped from leaving Kinshasa.
